On the first Thursday of every month, people brought broken things to the community hall.

They arrived carrying lamps, radios, jackets, bicycles, and occasionally objects that were difficult to classify. Once, a woman brought a wooden box with no lid and asked whether anyone could make it close properly. Nobody understood what the box was for, including the woman. It had belonged to her father, and she wanted to keep it without having to explain why.

The repair table occupied the far wall, beneath a clock that had stopped at 2:17. Nobody fixed the clock. There was a joke that repairing it would leave everyone with one less reason to gather.

Marta worked at the table nearest the door. She had retired from the post office five years earlier and knew how to mend almost anything made of cloth. People tended to tell her things while she sewed. Perhaps it was because she kept her eyes on her work, or because the small, steady movement of a needle made a silence easier to bear.

One rainy evening, a boy of about twelve brought in a blue backpack. Its zipper had lost several teeth, and one strap was held on with a safety pin.

“Can you fix it?” he asked.

“I can fix the strap,” Marta said. “The zipper might need replacing.”

He looked at the floor. “How long?”

“Next month, probably.”

“I need it for school.”

Marta turned the bag over. The canvas was thin where it rubbed against the boy’s back. She could replace the zipper, but the new one would be stronger than the fabric holding it. She could mend the strap, and another seam would pull loose. It was the kind of repair that asked a question nobody liked: when did fixing something become a way of refusing to see that it was worn out?

“Sit down,” she said.

The boy took a chair while she searched through a tin of buckles and buttons. Around them, the hall filled with familiar sounds: a screwdriver slipping against a screw, the snap of a switched-on lamp, the kettle beginning to boil. At the next table, Mr. Adeyemi was trying to persuade a toaster to release a piece of bread. He had brought bread because, as he pointed out, there was no other way to know whether the toaster worked.

Marta cut away the safety pin and threaded a needle with blue cord.

“Is it your only bag?” she asked.

The boy nodded.

“Then I’ll make it last until we find you another.”

He watched her stitch. She used short loops, drawing the loose strap tight against the canvas. When she finished, she made him put the backpack on and walk to the other end of the hall. The strap held. He came back trying not to smile.

“What about the zipper?”

“For now, put your books in a plastic bag inside it. Rain can get through those gaps.”

He seemed disappointed, but he thanked her. As he was leaving, he stopped beside a table of donated objects. Most of them were there because their owners had not wanted to carry them home: a chipped mug, three picture frames, a bicycle bell, a yellow scarf. There was also a sturdy black backpack, missing only the pull from one zipper. Marta had not noticed it.

The boy picked it up. “Is this for anyone?”

“If it’s on that table, it’s for whoever needs it.”

He tested the zipper. It opened and closed with a little tug. Then he looked at the blue backpack still hanging from his shoulder.

“You can take both,” Marta said.

“I know.” He set the black one down. “I like mine.”

After he left, Marta told the others about the bag. Mr. Adeyemi said the boy would be back for the black one when the blue one gave out. Someone else said he ought to have taken it now. Marta was inclined to agree. Still, the strap had held when he walked across the hall, and it would probably hold on the way to school.

The following month, he returned with both backpacks. The blue one had lost a buckle. The black one had a bright red shoelace tied to its zipper.

“My sister’s using this,” he said, placing the black bag on Marta’s table. “One of the straps is too long for her.”

While Marta shortened it, he stood beside her and examined the other repairs. A volunteer showed him how to replace the battery in a wall clock. They tried it, but the hands stayed where they were. The volunteer took the clock apart again, and the boy stayed to help.

Over the next few months, he came in to borrow tools, bring them back, and ask what various small parts were called. Sometimes he brought his sister. She liked the kettle and was particularly good at finding lost screws on the floor.

By autumn, the blue backpack was mostly stitches. Marta had repaired the zipper after all, along with both straps and a hole in the bottom. One evening the boy arrived with the bag in his hands rather than on his back. The canvas had torn beside her newest seam.

“Can you do it again?” he asked.

Marta spread it on the table. She found a sound piece of fabric farther down and considered how far she might extend the patch. Then she noticed the boy was watching her hands. He was older than he had been in the spring; she could see it in the patient way he waited for an answer.

“I can try,” she said. “Come and hold this edge for me.”

She gave him a needle of his own. His first stitch was crooked, and so were the next few. Marta showed him how to pull the thread through without bunching the cloth. They worked until the hall caretaker began putting chairs away.

When they were done, the patch covered nearly half the back of the bag. The boy put it on. Marta checked the seams while he turned around, then let him go.

The next Thursday, someone finally brought a ladder and took down the stopped clock. Mr. Adeyemi cleaned its contacts and fitted a fresh battery. At first nothing happened. Then the second hand moved.

By the time they hung it up, everyone was late going home.
